o: Find the shortest length L such that some sequence of L dice rolls (faces 1..k) never appears as a subsequence of the observed rolls. Greedy insight: if we can slice the array into R consecutive blocks each containing every face 1..k, then every sequence of length R is realizable (pick its ith face from block i), while some sequence of length R+1 is not (the next block lacks at least one face). Answer = R + 1. Example 1 splits into [4,2,1,2,3,3,2,4,1] blocks {1,2,3,4}, {1,2,3,4}, {2,4,1}? — counting completes: 2 full blocks plus a partial, giving 3.
k: Every length-L sequence is a subsequence iff the rolls can be partitioned into L consecutive blocks each containing all k faces.
Greedy: cut a block as soon as all k faces have been seen since the last cut.

a.i: Scan once, collecting faces of the current block in a set; when the set reaches size k, a block completes (increment count, clear set). After R completed blocks, every length-R sequence is achievable by choosing faces block by block, but any length-(R+1) sequence needs a kth block containing all faces, which the remainder cannot guarantee — indeed the face missing from the partial remainder extended by construction defeats it. Hence answer R + 1.
s: Maintain a set of faces seen in the current block and a block counter.
Add each roll to the set; when the set size hits k, increment the counter and clear the set.
a.t: O(n) — single scan with O(1) amortized set operations (set size never exceeds k).

w: The correctness argument (blocks => all sequences of that length exist; incomplete tail => some sequence of length+1 missing) is the crux — practice stating it crisply. Pitfall: answering 'blocks' instead of 'blocks + 1', or trying complicated subsequence automata unnecessarily. Follow-up: count how many distinct sequences of length L are missing, or handle a weighted die.
